Guided Project: Scales and Facets

CIS-3901 · Module 13

Author

Sudip Amgain

Published

November 15, 2026

My data

The Fairness section uses an Adult income dataset with 5,000 observations. The plots examine income, sex, race, capital gains, and weekly working hours.

put_in_place("fairness.csv")
put_in_place("sports.csv")

fairness <- read_csv("data/fairness.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
sports <- read_csv("data/sports.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

if (looks_damaged(fairness) || looks_damaged(sports)) {
  stop("One of your data files looks damaged (each row in one column): it ",
       "may have been re-saved by a spreadsheet app. Ask your instructor ",
       "for a fresh copy.", call. = FALSE)
}

# PART A · FAIRNESS ==========================================================

# A0 · See it update ---------------------------------------------------------
# A ready count plot of one of your Fairness columns. Nothing to code.
# YOUR TURN (kickoff): change one word in the title, then render the report
# and the slides, and find your word on both pages.

Part A · Fairness

A0 · See it update

a0_column <- pick_a_column(fairness)

a0 <- ggplot(fairness, aes(y = .data[[a0_column]])) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "My Fairness Plot", x = "Count", y = a0_column)

show_plot(a0)

I changed the plot title and checked that the updated title appeared in both the report and slides.

A1 · Label it

a_data <- fairness %>%
  mutate(
    group = sex,
    has_outcome = income == ">50K"
  )

a_data %>%
  count(group, has_outcome) %>%
  print(n = Inf)
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  group  has_outcome     n
  <chr>  <lgl>       <int>
1 Female FALSE        1477
2 Female TRUE          180
3 Male   FALSE        2328
4 Male   TRUE         1015
a1_base <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "Share of the group", y = NULL, fill = "Income >50K")


a1 <- a1_base +
  labs(
    title = "Share Earning Above $50K by Sex",
    subtitle = "Adult income dataset (n = 5,000)",
    x = "Percentage of each sex group",
    y = "Sex",
    fill = "Income above $50K"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent)

show_plot(a1)

The legend title was the label I changed most because the original TRUE and FALSE values were not very descriptive. I changed it to “Income above $50K” to make the outcome clearer. I also added a descriptive title and percentage axis labels. A reader can understand the comparison without needing additional explanations.

A2 · Choose a scale

# YOUR TURN: remove the # signs below, then replace each ___.
sum(fairness$capital_gain <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 4563
a2 <- fairness %>%
   filter(capital_gain > 0) %>%
   ggplot(aes(x = capital_gain)) +
   geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
   scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
   labs(title = "Distribution of Capital Gains", x = "Capital gain (dollars, log scale)", y = "Count")

# YOUR TURN: one sentence. Why this scale for this column?
a2_reason <- "Capital gains are highly right-skewed, so a log scale makes the distribution easier to examine."

show_plot(a2)

I used a logarithmic scale because capital gains are highly right-skewed. It makes smaller positive values easier to examine alongside larger values. I excluded 4,563 zero or negative values because they cannot be displayed on a logarithmic scale.

A3 · Facet it: fixed or free

# YOUR TURN 1: replace "replace me" with your second column (no quotes).
a3_rates <- a_data %>%
  mutate(panel = race) %>%
  drop_na(has_outcome) %>%
  add_count(panel, name = "panel_n") %>%
  mutate(panel = paste0(panel, " (n = ", scales::comma(panel_n), ")")) %>%
  group_by(panel, group) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), rate = mean(has_outcome), .groups = "drop")

a3_rates
# A tibble: 10 × 4
   panel                        group      n   rate
   <chr>                        <chr>  <int>  <dbl>
 1 Amer-Indian-Eskimo (n = 47)  Female    18 0.0556
 2 Amer-Indian-Eskimo (n = 47)  Male      29 0.138 
 3 Asian-Pac-Islander (n = 156) Female    53 0.132 
 4 Asian-Pac-Islander (n = 156) Male     103 0.340 
 5 Black (n = 479)              Female   236 0.0551
 6 Black (n = 479)              Male     243 0.181 
 7 Other (n = 42)               Female    16 0.0625
 8 Other (n = 42)               Male      26 0.154 
 9 White (n = 4,276)            Female  1334 0.118 
10 White (n = 4,276)            Male    2942 0.315 
a3_fixed <- ggplot(a3_rates, aes(x = group, y = rate)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Income Above $50K by Sex and Race",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Percentage earning above $50K"
  )

a3_free <- a3_fixed + facet_wrap(vars(panel), scales="free_y")

# YOUR TURN 3: which one would you publish, "fixed" or "free_y"? Why?
a3_choice <- "fixed"
a3_reason <- "I chose fixed scales because using the same percentage range across all race panels makes comparisons between racial groups easier and more honest."

show_plot(a3_fixed)
show_plot(a3_free)

I chose fixed scales because using the same percentage range makes comparisons between race groups easier. Males had a higher percentage earning above $50,000 in every race group. Some groups had small sample sizes, such as Other (42 people) and American Indian-Eskimo (47 people).

A4 · Compared to what?

# YOUR TURN 1: remove the # signs below, then replace each ___: the column
# with your groups, two of its values, and your numeric column.
a4_clouds <- a_data %>%
   filter(sex %in% c("Female", "Male")) %>%
   make_clouds(group, hours_per_week)

# YOUR TURN 2: remove the # signs below, then replace each ___.
a4 <- ggplot(a4_clouds, aes(x = group, y = value)) +
   geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.2) +
   facet_wrap(~ kind) +
   labs(title = "Weekly Working Hours by Sex", x = "Sex", y = "Hours worked per week")

show_plot(a4)

The individual values overlap considerably, meaning both groups have a wide range of working hours. However, the resampled group means are clearly separated, with males having a higher average weekly working time around 40 hours. This shows that individual differences can overlap even when group averages are different.

A5 · Color for every reader

# YOUR TURN: remove the # signs below, then replace each ___ (the same
# column in both places, so its name is on the axis too).
a5 <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = sex, fill = sex)) +
   geom_bar() +
   scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.8) +
   labs(title = "Number of People by Sex", x = "Count", y = "Sex", fill = "Sex")

show_plot(a5)
# See it: your plot as a reader with red-green color blindness might see it.
show_plot(simulate_plot(a5, "Red-green (deuteranopia)"))
color_check(a5)
2 colors. The red-green simulations come from a validated model;
the blue-yellow one is an approximation.
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  view                      smallest_difference at_least_20
  <chr>                                   <dbl> <chr>      
1 Red-green (deuteranopia)                 99.5 Yes        
2 Red-green (protanopia)                  119.  Yes        
3 Blue-yellow (approximate)                81.3 Yes        
show_plot(simulate_plot(a5, "Red-green (protanopia)"))
show_plot(simulate_plot(a5, "Blue-yellow (approximate)"))

I colored the plot by sex to distinguish female and male adults. All three color vision simulations passed the color check, and the categories remained distinguishable in the simulated views.

Part B · Sports

B1 · Label it

b_data <- sports %>%
  mutate(
    group = surface,
    has_outcome = minutes > 120,
    value = minutes
  )

b_data %>%
  count(group, has_outcome) %>%
  print(n = Inf)
# A tibble: 8 × 3
  group has_outcome     n
  <chr> <lgl>       <int>
1 Clay  FALSE         395
2 Clay  TRUE          108
3 Clay  NA            132
4 Grass FALSE         411
5 Grass TRUE           97
6 Hard  FALSE         960
7 Hard  TRUE          309
8 Hard  NA              1
b1_base <- ggplot(
  b_data,
  aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)
) + geom_bar(position = "fill") + 
  labs(
    x = "Share of the group",
    y = "Court surface",
    fill = "Match over 120 minutes"
  )

b1 <- b1_base +
  labs(
    title = "Long Matches by Court Surface",
    subtitle = "WTA Grand Slam matches, 2018-2022",
    x = "Share of matches (%)",
    y = "Court surface",
    fill = "Match over 120 minutes"
  ) + 
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent)
  

show_plot(b1)

I changed the x-axis label the most because the plot shows percentages rather than raw counts. I labeled it “Share of matches (%)” to make that clear. The title, subtitle, and legend also explain what is being compared, so a reader can understand the plot without additional explanation.

B2 · Choose a scale

sum(is.na(sports$winner_rank))
[1] 5
sum(sports$winner_rank <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 0
b2 <- sports %>%
  filter(!is.na(winner_rank), winner_rank > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = winner_rank)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Winning Player Rankings",
    x = "Winner ranking (log scale)",
    y = "Number of matches"
  )

b2_reason <- "Player rankings are right-skewed, with many lower numerical rankings and fewer very large rankings. A log scale makes the distribution easier to examine."

show_plot(b2)

I used a logarithmic scale because winner rankings are right-skewed. It makes the distribution easier to examine by showing smaller and larger rankings together. Five observations with missing rankings were removed, while no zero or negative values needed to be excluded.

B3 · Facet it: fixed or free

b3_rates <- b_data %>%
  mutate(
    panel = as.character(str_sub(as.character(tourney_date), 1, 4))
  ) %>%
  drop_na(has_outcome) %>%
  add_count(panel, name = "panel_n") %>%
  mutate(panel = paste0(
    panel, " (n = ", scales::comma(panel_n), ")"
  )) %>%
  group_by(panel, group) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    rate = mean(has_outcome),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

b3_rates
# A tibble: 13 × 4
   panel          group     n  rate
   <chr>          <chr> <int> <dbl>
 1 2018 (n = 507) Clay    126 0.159
 2 2018 (n = 507) Grass   127 0.205
 3 2018 (n = 507) Hard    254 0.256
 4 2019 (n = 506) Clay    125 0.192
 5 2019 (n = 506) Grass   127 0.189
 6 2019 (n = 506) Hard    254 0.232
 7 2020 (n = 381) Clay    127 0.260
 8 2020 (n = 381) Hard    254 0.248
 9 2021 (n = 505) Clay    125 0.248
10 2021 (n = 505) Grass   127 0.189
11 2021 (n = 505) Hard    253 0.221
12 2022 (n = 381) Grass   127 0.181
13 2022 (n = 381) Hard    254 0.260
b3_fixed <- ggplot(b3_rates, aes(x = group, y = rate)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Long Matches by Surface Across Years",
    x = "Court surface",
    y = "Percentage of matches over 120 minutes (%)"
  )

b3_free <- b3_fixed +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel), scales = "free_y")

b3_choice <- "fixed"
b3_reason <- "I chose fixed scales because all panels represent percentages. Using the same scale makes year-to-year comparisons easier."

show_plot(b3_fixed)
show_plot(b3_free)

I chose fixed scales because they allow readers to compare match percentages across years using the same y-axis range. This makes differences easier to compare, but smaller changes may be harder to notice. The smallest panels were 2020 and 2022, with 381 matches each. Hard courts had the highest percentage of long matches in 2018, 2019, and 2022, while Clay had the highest in 2020 and 2021. These are differences in the data, not evidence of causes.

B4 · Compared to what?

b4_clouds <- b_data %>%
  filter(surface %in% c("Hard", "Clay")) %>%
  make_clouds(group, minutes)

b4 <- ggplot(b4_clouds, aes(x = group, y = value)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ kind) +
  labs(title = "Match Duration by Court Surface", x = "Court surface", y = "Match duration (minutes)")

show_plot(b4)

The individual values overlap considerably, meaning Clay and Hard court matches can have similar durations, with plenty of variation within each surface. The resampled means are also very close, showing that the average match durations for the two surfaces are nearly the same, even though individual match lengths vary widely.

B5 · Color for every reader

b5 <- ggplot(b_data, aes(y = surface, fill = surface)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Number of Matches by Court Surface", x = "Count", y = "Court Surface", fill = "Court Surface")


show_plot(b5)
show_plot(simulate_plot(b5, "Red-green (deuteranopia)"))
color_check(b5)
3 colors. The red-green simulations come from a validated model;
the blue-yellow one is an approximation.
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  view                      smallest_difference at_least_20
  <chr>                                   <dbl> <chr>      
1 Red-green (deuteranopia)                 30.5 Yes        
2 Red-green (protanopia)                   41.1 Yes        
3 Blue-yellow (approximate)                29.7 Yes        
show_plot(simulate_plot(b5, "Red-green (protanopia)"))
show_plot(simulate_plot(b5, "Blue-yellow (approximate)"))

I colored by the surface column to distinguish Clay, Grass, and Hard courts. I used the Viridis color scale because it provides distinguishable colors. My plot passed the color check without needing to change the categories. In all three simulated views, the categories remain distinguishable.

One thing I tried in my slides, and why

I used a finding-based headline instead of a general topic title: “Males had a higher percentage of adults earning above $50,000 in every race group.” This tells the audience the main finding before they look at the chart and makes the comparison easier to follow.
